chartPlan.title: One dollar in rupees, from fixed pegs to a managed float
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The headline everyone knows and almost everyone misreads: the rupee's long slide against the dollar.
chartPlan.howToRead: A steep rise means fewer dollars per rupee; the flat periods are pegs, not stability.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming all points are market-determined: pre-1993 rates were fixed by policy.

chartPlan.title: The rupee's dollar fall came in bursts, not a steady slide
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The slide was never steady; it came in bursts, and naming the decades shows the rupee has been broadly stable against the dollar for long stretches.
chartPlan.howToRead: Each bar shows the percentage loss in the rupee’s dollar value over that decade.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Missing the 2000s when the rupee barely moved; the slide is not monotonic.

chartPlan.title: The rupee fell most against the dollar, not equally against every currency
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The rupee did not weaken evenly against everything; it fell hardest against the dollar and far less against the pound and yen, so much of the 'weakness' is really dollar strength.
chartPlan.howToRead: A falling line means the rupee lost value against that currency; lines clustered near 50-60 mean similar weakening.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Comparing the exact levels across currencies without noting the different base dates.

chartPlan.title: The rupee was mid-pack in a strong-dollar world
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The most freeing chart in the article: a currency's price is relative, and against a strong dollar almost every currency lost ground, with the rupee sitting mid-pack among emerging markets, far from the worst.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bars to the right lost more value against the dollar; negative bars gained.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Reading this as a ranking of economic strength; it’s a snapshot of dollar strength over a specific period.

chartPlan.title: Reserves grew from a few weeks of imports to a $686 billion buffer
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The 1991 devaluation was not a choice, it was a near-default: India had almost run out of dollars.
chartPlan.howToRead: The line starts near zero and rises steeply after the 1990s; dips indicate stress episodes.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Ignoring the log scale; the visual growth is even faster in reality.

chartPlan.title: The current-account deficit is where rupee crises begin
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Behind every rupee crisis is the same trigger: India spending more abroad than it earns, so it must pull in foreign money to bridge the gap, and when that money stops, the rupee breaks.
chartPlan.howToRead: Negative bars (below zero) mean India spent more than it earned; deeper red preceded the 1991, 2013 and 2022 stresses.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A current-account deficit is not always bad; it becomes dangerous only when financing dries up.

chartPlan.title: Interest rates rose in crises, but they do not set the rupee alone
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The interest-rate backdrop to the whole story: sky-high in the controlled era, spiking to defend the rupee in crises, low and steadier today.
chartPlan.howToRead: The line is the central bank’s policy rate; spikes coincide with high inflation or currency defence.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Comparing to today’s repo rate; the early series may use a different policy instrument.

chartPlan.title: A narrow monthly range shows the rupee is managed, not freely floating
chartPlan.whyShowThis: A genuine free float would swing wildly; the rupee's tight monthly band is the fingerprint of management.
chartPlan.howToRead: The shaded area between month-high and month-low widens during crises; large swings mean the RBI let the rupee move.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming a narrow range means the RBI fixes the rate; it only limits extreme volatility.

chartPlan.title: RBI spot intervention: buying dollars in calm, selling in stress
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The central bank says it only curbs volatility; its dollar buying and selling shows what that means month to month.
chartPlan.howToRead: Positive values are net dollar purchases (accumulating reserves); negative are net sales (defending the rupee).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A single large negative month does not mean the RBI is panicking; it is often responding to a spike in outflows.

chartPlan.title: Hot portfolio money is the tide the RBI leans against
chartPlan.whyShowThis: RBI research finds the rupee is moved mainly by volatile foreign portfolio flows, not by inflation; intervention leans against that tide.
chartPlan.howToRead: Portfolio inflows and RBI dollar buying often move opposite; outflows coincide with heavy RBI selling.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming the two series cancel each other perfectly; intervention is a dampener, not a full offset.

chartPlan.title: The RBI's forward book is committed defence, not free reserves
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Modern intervention increasingly hides in the forwards market, off the visible spot reserves.
chartPlan.howToRead: A growing negative number means the RBI has committed to sell more dollars in the future; it signals heavy defence.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Treating a large negative forward book as a reserve; it is a future liability, not an asset.

chartPlan.title: FDI is slower; FPI is the money that whipsaws the rupee
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Not all foreign money behaves the same: direct investment is sticky and builds factories, portfolio money is fast and can leave in a week, and it is the second kind that whipsaws the rupee.
chartPlan.howToRead: FDI bars are smoother and usually positive; FPI bars swing wildly from positive to negative.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Comparing the absolute scales directly; FDI monthly flows are smaller but steadier.

chartPlan.title: The rupee often moves with the global dollar cycle
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The rupee's worst stretches line up with a globally strong dollar, not with India-specific news: when the dollar rises against all emerging markets, the rupee falls with the pack.
chartPlan.howToRead: When the dollar index (blue) rises, the rupee index (orange) tends to fall; mirror images are common.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Reading this as a perfect mirror; short-term deviations are frequent because capital flows can diverge.

chartPlan.title: Against the dollar it collapsed; in real trade-weighted terms, much less
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The single chart that overturns the panic: against the dollar the rupee fell to a third, but in real trade-weighted terms it barely moved.
chartPlan.howToRead: The red line (REER) is near 100; the blue line (vs USD) is at 34; the gap is inflation.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming REER = 100 means the rupee is fairly valued; it just means the nominal fall roughly matched the inflation gap.

chartPlan.title: The long real rupee: overvaluation, 1991 correction, managed range
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Zoom out to half a century and the real rupee tells a story of correction, not collapse.
chartPlan.howToRead: REER started overvalued near 120 in 1975, dropped sharply in 1991, and then ranged between 90 and 110.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Comparing the exact index values now and in 1975; the base year is 1985=100.

chartPlan.title: Higher Indian inflation is the long-run pressure on the rupee
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The engine under the whole story: since 1991 Indian prices have risen far more than American prices, and a currency cannot hold a fixed dollar value while its prices outrun the other country's.
chartPlan.howToRead: India’s line (blue) rises steeply; the US line (orange) stays modest; the widening gap is inflation differential.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Ignoring that 1991 is the base year; the cumulative inflation story starts from there.

chartPlan.title: Inflation explains much of the fall, but not the overshoot
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Inflation differences explain the direction of the fall, but not all of it, and the gap is the honest part of the story.
chartPlan.howToRead: The actual rate (blue) rises faster than the PPP-implied rate (orange); the difference is the 'excess' depreciation.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking PPP is a daily driver; it’s a long-run anchor, and short-run deviations are large.

chartPlan.title: The inflation gap matters over decades, not every month
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The mechanism under the whole story: India has run higher inflation than the US for decades, so the rupee must fall to keep trade competitive.
chartPlan.howToRead: Blue (India inflation) is almost always above orange (US inflation); that persistent gap is the fundamental force.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A single month where US inflation exceeds India’s does not change the long-run trend.

chartPlan.title: The same exports look different in rupees and dollars
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The same exports look like a miracle in rupees and a steady climb in dollars; the entire gap is the exchange rate.
chartPlan.howToRead: The log scale turns a constant proportionate gap into parallel lines; the distance between the lines is the rupee’s depreciation.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Reading the gap as a parallel shift; on a linear scale the rupee line would outpace the dollar line dramatically.

chartPlan.title: A banked rupee did not behave like cash under a mattress
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The reframe that defuses the debasement panic: nobody holds wealth in cash, and a banked rupee kept its purchasing power.
chartPlan.howToRead: The green line (real value) ends above 1; the orange line (cost of living) runs parallel; the blue line (nominal) soars.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming the real gain is large; it’s modest and highly dependent on the inflation index.

chartPlan.title: Bank deposits did not always beat inflation
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The honest other half of the savings story: in the controlled decades the interest a deposit paid was less than inflation, so even the careful saver lost ground, until liberalisation turned real rates positive.
chartPlan.howToRead: When the line is above zero, the deposit rate beat inflation; below zero it lost purchasing power.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: The 1970s–80s were not all negative; the line spiked positive briefly, but the general trend was repressive.

chartPlan.title: Oil in rupees: global crude plus exchange-rate pain
chartPlan.whyShowThis: India imports most of its oil in dollars, so a weaker rupee raises the pump price even when world oil is flat.
chartPlan.howToRead: The rupee line (blue) rises much faster than the dollar line (orange); the extra slope is depreciation.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: This is an index; actual petrol prices include central and state taxes that can dominate the move.

chartPlan.title: India's oil bill is the biggest recurring dollar drain
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Oil is India's single biggest import and the main reason a weak rupee feeds straight into inflation.
chartPlan.howToRead: The line jumps in global oil spikes (1973, 2008, 2022) and plateaus when prices fall.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Comparing oil import values over time without adjusting for volume growth; the price component is only part of the story.

chartPlan.title: Remittances are the other side of depreciation
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Depreciation is not all cost: India is the world's largest remittance recipient, and every weaker rupee turns each sent dollar into more rupees at home.
chartPlan.howToRead: The line soaring to $138 billion shows the scale; a weaker rupee amplifies the local purchasing power of each dollar.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Remittance data are in dollars; the rupee value is many times higher due to the exchange rate.

chartPlan.title: The goods trade gap keeps India hunting for dollars
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Underneath the currency sits a simple fact: India buys more from the world than it sells, so it constantly needs dollars, which is why capital flows and remittances matter so much.
chartPlan.howToRead: The gap between imports (orange) and exports (blue) has widened over time; a larger trade deficit means more dependence on foreign capital.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Treating the trade deficit as a pure negative; it partly reflects India’s growth and investment needs.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: An exchange rate is the price of one currency written in another currency. If the rupee-dollar rate is 90, one dollar costs 90 rupees; if it moves to 95, the same dollar has become more expensive for someone paying in rupees.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Every part of the rupee story starts from understanding that the rupee-dollar rate is a relative price. It is not, by itself, a scorecard of national strength.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Devaluation is an official reset of the currency’s price when the exchange rate is fixed or tightly pegged. If the government says the old rate is no longer defensible and announces a weaker rate, that is devaluation, not ordinary market trading.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The rupee’s falls in 1949, 1966 and 1991 were policy decisions, not market moves. Knowing the difference stops you from misreading the pre-1993 chart.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Depreciation means a currency buys less of another currency than before. If one dollar moves from 80 rupees to 90 rupees, the rupee has depreciated against the dollar because you now need 10 more rupees to buy the same dollar.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: After 1993 the rupee floats with management, so most headline falls are depreciation, not deliberate cuts. The word tells you direction, not cause: inflation, dollar strength, capital outflows and oil can all be part of the same move.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: NEER, or nominal effective exchange rate, is the rupee measured against a basket of trading-partner currencies instead of only the dollar. The weights reflect trade links, so bigger trading partners matter more in the index.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The dollar-rupee rate is just one pair. NEER tells a broader story, but it still does not adjust for inflation.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: REER, or real effective exchange rate, starts with the trade-weighted currency basket and then adjusts for inflation differences. If Indian prices rise faster than partner-country prices, REER asks whether the exchange rate moved enough to offset that price gap.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: REER is the closest chart here to external competitiveness. It is much flatter than the rupee-dollar line, which is why the dollar chart exaggerates the real collapse story.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services goes up, reducing what each rupee buys.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Persistently higher Indian inflation than US inflation is the fundamental reason the rupee had to fall over time.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The current account adds up India’s regular earning and spending with the world: goods trade, services trade, income flows and transfers such as remittances. A deficit means India is spending more foreign currency than it is earning through these channels.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: A current-account deficit is not automatically a crisis, because investment inflows can finance it. It becomes a rupee problem when the gap is large and the foreign money needed to fund it becomes nervous or scarce.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: FPI is foreign money invested in Indian stocks, bonds and other financial assets. It can enter quickly when global investors like India or emerging markets, and leave quickly when rates, risk appetite or the dollar move against them.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: FPI outflows are one of the fastest channels through which global stress hits the rupee. They matter more for short-run currency pressure than a factory investment that takes years to build.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: FDI is foreign investment tied to ownership and a business presence, such as a factory, subsidiary, acquisition or long-term project. It can still rise and fall, but it is harder to reverse overnight than selling a bond or share.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: FDI is the patient-money side of the capital-flow story. Comparing it with FPI helps explain why some foreign flows whipsaw the rupee while others do not.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The forward book is the RBI’s net set of promises to buy or sell dollars at future dates. A negative number means the RBI has promised to deliver more dollars in the future than it will receive.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Forwards can support the rupee today without immediately reducing headline reserves. But they are not free reserves; they are future dollar commitments that must be settled, rolled or offset later.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The impossible trinity says a country cannot fully have all three at once: a fixed exchange rate, completely free capital movement and an independent monetary policy. If money can move freely and the exchange rate is fixed, the central bank loses room to set interest rates for domestic needs.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India chose a managed float and still has some capital controls, which preserves the RBI’s ability to set interest rates independently.

proseRules: No AI tells, no elaborate metaphors, no em-dashes.
Every number must come from lockedNumbers in the evidence packet.
No speculation about policy outcomes or future exchange-rate levels.
All headings are reader-questions in markdown H2.
Use ‘one visible reason in this data’ instead of claiming causation.
Never call GDP a measure of income; define GVA and GDP correctly if used.
Write for a sharp sixteen-year-old; define jargon instantly.

plannedCharts.title: One dollar in rupees, from fixed pegs to a managed float
plannedCharts.subtitle: What one US dollar has cost in rupees since Independence, separating fixed pegs and devaluations from the later managed market rate.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This is the headline number, but it must be read as regime history: fixed pegs first, one-off devaluations next, and a managed float after 1993.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee's dollar fall came in bursts, not a steady slide
plannedCharts.unit: % of value lost vs the dollar
plannedCharts.subtitle: How much dollar value the rupee lost in each decade, showing that the largest falls came in specific crisis and adjustment periods.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The rupee did not weaken at a constant pace; decade bars show where the real breaks happened.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee fell most against the dollar, not equally against every currency
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee's value against the dollar, euro, pound and yen since 1999, all indexed to show that the bilateral story depends on the other currency too.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A currency is always a pair, and the rupee-dollar headline hides how differently the rupee moved against other major currencies.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee was mid-pack in a strong-dollar world
plannedCharts.unit: % of value lost vs the dollar, 2000-2025
plannedCharts.subtitle: How much major currencies lost against the US dollar from 2000 to 2025, placing the rupee beside peers instead of judging it in isolation.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The dollar was unusually strong over this period, so the right test is whether the rupee was an outlier, not whether it fell at all.

plannedCharts.title: Reserves grew from a few weeks of imports to a $686 billion buffer
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's foreign-exchange reserves including gold, showing the 1991 near-empty cupboard and the much larger modern cushion.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Reserves are the difference between depreciation under pressure and a full external payments crisis.

plannedCharts.title: The current-account deficit is where rupee crises begin
plannedCharts.subtitle: The gap between what India earns from the world and what it spends abroad, before capital flows cover or fail to cover it.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A current-account deficit is the recurring place where trade, oil, services, remittances and capital flows meet the rupee.

plannedCharts.title: Each rupee crisis had a different mix of pressures
plannedCharts.subtitle: A curated stress scorecard across major rupee episodes, combining devaluation/depreciation, external deficit, reserves, hot money or dollar pressure, oil and policy stress.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This is the adversarial check: if the article says many things move the rupee, crisis episodes should show different mixes of those things.

plannedCharts.title: Interest rates rose in crises, but they do not set the rupee alone
plannedCharts.subtitle: The RBI's main policy rate across regimes, showing how monetary policy interacts with inflation, growth and currency defence.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Rates matter for capital flows, but raising rates to defend the rupee has domestic costs.

plannedCharts.title: A narrow monthly range shows the rupee is managed, not freely floating
plannedCharts.subtitle: The strongest and weakest rupee-dollar quote within each month, exposing how tightly the exchange rate is often smoothed.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The monthly high-low band is a visible fingerprint of a managed float.

plannedCharts.title: RBI spot intervention: buying dollars in calm, selling in stress
plannedCharts.subtitle: The RBI's net spot dollar purchases and sales, the most visible part of how it smooths the rupee.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Intervention data shows currency management in actual dollars bought and sold.

plannedCharts.title: Hot portfolio money is the tide the RBI leans against
plannedCharts.subtitle: Foreign portfolio flows beside RBI spot intervention, showing why fast-moving capital matters for rupee volatility.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: RBI research points to portfolio flows as a central source of rupee volatility; this chart shows the mechanism.

plannedCharts.title: The RBI's forward book is committed defence, not free reserves
plannedCharts.subtitle: The RBI net forward dollar position, where selling dollars for future delivery can support the rupee without immediately reducing spot reserves.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Forwards reveal currency defence that does not immediately show up as a fall in visible reserves.

plannedCharts.title: FDI is slower; FPI is the money that whipsaws the rupee
plannedCharts.subtitle: Foreign direct investment beside portfolio flows, separating stickier long-term money from fast-moving market money.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Not all foreign capital behaves alike, and the rupee reacts most to the money that can leave fastest.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee often moves with the global dollar cycle
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee-dollar rate beside a broad emerging-market dollar index, showing the global driver behind many rupee moves.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Many rupee falls happen when the dollar strengthens broadly, not only when Indian news worsens.

plannedCharts.title: Rupee volatility reveals how tightly the RBI held it
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee-dollar rate split into de-facto management regimes, using volatility as a clue to how freely the rupee was allowed to move.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The RBI does not announce a target band, so realised volatility is one way to infer how tightly the rupee was managed.

plannedCharts.title: Against the dollar it collapsed; in real trade-weighted terms, much less
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee measured three ways since 1994: against the dollar, against trading partners, and after adjusting for inflation.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This is the core reveal: the dollar chart is not the same as the inflation-adjusted trade-weighted rupee.

plannedCharts.title: The long real rupee: overvaluation, 1991 correction, managed range
plannedCharts.subtitle: RBI's long NEER and REER history, chain-linked across the discontinued 36-country basket and the newer 40-country basket.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The half-century view shows correction and managed fluctuation, not a simple collapse.

plannedCharts.title: Higher Indian inflation is the long-run pressure on the rupee

series.label: Cost of living in the US

plannedCharts.subtitle: The cumulative cost of living in India and the US since 1991, showing why a fixed dollar rate would have become hard to sustain.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A country with persistently higher inflation usually needs a weaker nominal currency over time to protect competitiveness.

plannedCharts.title: Inflation explains much of the fall, but not the overshoot
plannedCharts.subtitle: The actual rupee-dollar rate beside a simple PPP-implied rate based only on the India-US inflation gap.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: PPP gives a useful baseline, and the gap from that baseline shows what inflation alone cannot explain.

plannedCharts.title: The inflation gap matters over decades, not every month
plannedCharts.subtitle: Year-on-year inflation in India and the US, useful for seeing direction but too noisy for month-by-month exchange-rate claims.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Annual inflation rates explain pressure over time, but the rupee does not mechanically follow each monthly inflation print.

plannedCharts.title: The same exports look different in rupees and dollars
plannedCharts.subtitle: India’s merchandise exports indexed in rupees and dollars, showing how depreciation changes the measurement without creating extra real exports.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The same trade flow can look explosive in rupees and much calmer in dollars because the exchange rate changes the unit of measurement.

plannedCharts.title: A banked rupee did not behave like cash under a mattress

series.label: One rupee in a bank deposit

plannedCharts.subtitle: One rupee rolled through a representative bank deposit since 1970, compared with the rising cost of living.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Households do not usually store long-term wealth as currency notes, so the saver’s question needs a return and inflation frame.

plannedCharts.title: Bank deposits did not always beat inflation
plannedCharts.subtitle: The representative bank deposit rate after subtracting inflation, showing why some decades were punishing for savers.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The savings counterfactual needs this caveat: over the full period deposits won, but not in every year.

plannedCharts.title: Oil in rupees: global crude plus exchange-rate pain
plannedCharts.subtitle: Brent crude indexed in dollars and rupees since 2000, showing how depreciation stacks on top of the world oil price.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Oil is the cleanest example of why a stable REER does not protect households from dollar-priced imports.

plannedCharts.title: India's oil bill is the biggest recurring dollar drain
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's annual petroleum import bill in dollars, the recurring expense that makes oil central to rupee vulnerability.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Oil is India’s largest recurring import bill and a major channel from rupee weakness to domestic prices.

plannedCharts.title: Dollar debt gets heavier when the rupee weakens
plannedCharts.subtitle: Dollar-denominated credit to Indian non-bank borrowers, where the rupee cost rises even if the dollar debt itself does not.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Depreciation hurts borrowers who earn in rupees but owe in dollars.

plannedCharts.title: Remittances are the other side of depreciation
plannedCharts.subtitle: Money sent home by Indians abroad, where each dollar converts into more rupees when the exchange rate weakens.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Depreciation has losers and beneficiaries; remittance recipients are one obvious beneficiary group.

plannedCharts.title: The goods trade gap keeps India hunting for dollars
plannedCharts.subtitle: Merchandise exports and imports in dollars, showing the persistent goods deficit that services, remittances and capital flows must finance.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The goods trade gap is the structural dollar need underneath the rupee debate.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
